name: Jorethang
tagline: Warm river town on the Rangeet, gateway to West Sikkim
meta_description: Jorethang, South Sikkim: Maghe Sankranti mela on the Rangeet, shared jeeps to Pelling, Namchi and Siliguri, where to eat, stay and honest 2026 costs.
summary: Jorethang is a busy market town of about 9,000 people on the Rangeet river at roughly 300 m, 18 km below Namchi. It is the main road junction for West and South Sikkim, with shared jeeps to Siliguri, Pelling and Gangtok, and hosts one of Sikkim's biggest fairs, the Maghe Sankranti mela, around 14 January.
intro: Jorethang sits low and warm on the Rangeet, the river that separates Sikkim from Darjeeling district for much of its length. At about 300 m it is one of the lowest towns in the state, with banana and mango trees, warm evenings and summer days that pass 30 °C. A bridge crosses the river to the Darjeeling side, and roads fan out from here to Namchi, Legship, Gyalshing, Pelling and Siliguri. The 2011 census counted 9,009 residents.

For travellers, Jorethang is mainly a junction. Shared jeeps from Siliguri bound for West Sikkim pass through, and its taxi stand sends vehicles to Pelling, Gyalshing, Namchi, Ravangla and Gangtok through the day. When NH10 is closed by monsoon slides, drivers from Siliguri and NJP often come via Darjeeling district down to Jorethang instead, so the town becomes even more important in July and August.

Jorethang has one big moment in the year. On the first day of the Nepali month of Magh, around 14 January, the Maghe Sankranti mela fills the riverbank with stalls, rides, music and families taking a holy dip in the Rangeet. Wikipedia dates the fair to 1961. Outside mela time, stop for an ATM, lunch, fuel and a stroll along the river, then head on into the hills.

story.title: Maghe Sankranti on the Rangeet since 1961
story.text: Maghe Sankranti marks the first day of Magh in the Nepali Vikram Samvat calendar, about 14 January, when the sun enters Makara, Capricorn, and the coldest part of winter starts to turn. Across Nepal and among Nepali-speaking communities in India it is a day for ritual baths at river confluences and for foods such as sesame sweets, yam, sweet potato and ghee. The Wikipedia article on Maghe Sankranti describes these customs, and the article on Jorethang records that the town's Maghe Sankranti mela has been held since 1961 and is one of the main festivals of the Nepali community in Sikkim. Jorethang's site on the Rangeet made it a natural gathering point: families from the villages of South and West Sikkim, and from across the river in Darjeeling district, came down to bathe, trade and meet. Over the decades the mela grew into a multi-day fair with stalls selling farm tools, clothes, handicrafts and food, cultural programmes and amusement rides. Dates and the programme are set each year by the organisers, so check current status before you travel.

little_known.fact: At about 300 m, Jorethang is among the lowest towns in Sikkim, a state that rises to 8,586 m at Kangchenjunga less than 100 km away.
The Rangeet, which flows past Jorethang, rises in the mountains of West Sikkim and later joins the Teesta at a confluence known as Tribeni, a popular picnic spot.
Wikipedia records Jorethang's literacy rate in the 2011 census as about 88.9 percent, above the Sikkim average of about 81.4 percent at the time.
little_known.source: Census of India 2011, via Wikipedia: Jorethang

highlights.title: Maghe Sankranti mela
highlights.text: Around 14 January the riverbank fills with a multi-day fair: stalls, rides, cultural programmes and families taking a dip in the Rangeet. Held since 1961, it is one of the biggest Nepali community festivals in Sikkim. Dates vary slightly; check current status before you travel.

highlights.title: The Rangeet riverfront
highlights.text: Walk down to the river in the late afternoon, when the heat eases and the light turns soft on the water. The Rangeet here is wide and green-blue in winter, brown and powerful in the monsoon, when you should keep well back from the banks.

highlights.title: Jeep junction for the west
highlights.text: Jorethang's taxi stand sends shared jeeps to Pelling, Gyalshing, Legship, Namchi, Ravangla, Gangtok and Siliguri. If you are travelling on a budget between South and West Sikkim, you will almost certainly change vehicles here.

highlights.title: Bazaar lunch stop
highlights.text: The market around the taxi stand has simple eateries serving thali, momos, chowmein and sel roti, plus fruit stalls with local bananas and oranges in season. A practical place for lunch, cash and fuel on long drives.

highlights.title: Up the valley to Legship
highlights.text: The road north along the Rangeet reaches Legship in Gyalshing district in about an hour, where the Kirateshwar Mahadev temple stands by the river. It is the usual road from Jorethang to Pelling.

how_to_reach.text: Shared jeeps run from Siliguri to Jorethang in about 3.5–4 hours for roughly ₹250–350 a seat, from Namchi in 40 minutes for about ₹50–80, and from Gangtok in 3.5–4 hours for around ₹300–400. Jeeps leave mostly in the morning. Fares are indicative; check current status before you travel.

A reserved small car from Namchi costs about ₹1,000–1,500 for the 18 km, and from Gangtok about ₹4,000–5,000. Jorethang to Pelling is about 50 km and 2 hours via Legship and Gyalshing, for roughly ₹2,500–3,500 one way.

About 95–100 km and 3.5–4 hours via NH10 to Melli and then along the river, for about ₹4,500–6,000 by reserved car. When NH10 is closed by monsoon slides, the alternative road comes via Darjeeling district straight down to Jorethang.

where_to_stay: Jorethang has a few simple budget hotels around the bazaar and taxi stand, with rooms at about ₹1,200–2,000, useful if you arrive late or leave early. We do not list them by name because standards change; ask us for current options. For most travellers we suggest staying in Namchi, 18 km and 40 minutes uphill, where Seven Hill Resort and Sobralia Hotels Casino Resort & Spa offer more comfort, cooler nights and mountain views.
tips: Book a mela-week room in Namchi early; Jorethang's few hotels fill with visiting families in mid-January.
Jorethang is hot from April to September, so plan a quick stop rather than a long walk in the afternoon.
Never wade into the Rangeet in the monsoon; the river rises fast after rain upstream.
Use Jorethang's ATMs before heading to remote villages in West or South Sikkim.
When NH10 is closed by monsoon slides, ask your driver about the Darjeeling–Jorethang road and allow extra time.

experiences.title: A day at Jorethang's Maghe Sankranti mela
experiences.best_time: Around 14 January (first of Magh), plus the following fair days
experiences.cost: Free entry; ≈ ₹300–800 for food and rides
experiences.summary: Join thousands of families on the Rangeet riverbank for Jorethang's Maghe Sankranti fair, held since 1961: a morning dip for the devout, then stalls, rides, folk music and festival food. The busiest and most cheerful day in South Sikkim's winter calendar.
body: Maghe Sankranti falls on the first of Magh in the Nepali calendar, about 14 January. In the early morning, devout families bathe in the Rangeet, then the day turns to celebration. Wikipedia records that the Jorethang mela dates from 1961 and is one of the main festivals of Sikkim's Nepali community.

Walk the stalls for farm tools, bamboo baskets, clothes, handicrafts and household goods, and eat the season's food: sesame and molasses sweets, sel roti, boiled yam and sweet potato. Cultural programmes, music and amusement rides run through the fair days, and the crowd draws families from across South and West Sikkim and the Darjeeling hills.

Arrive by mid-morning for the best atmosphere, and keep valuables close in the crowds. Traffic slows on all roads into town, so allow extra time and consider staying in Namchi. The fair programme and dates are set by the organisers each year; check current status before you travel.

faqs.q: When is the Jorethang Maghe Mela?
faqs.a: It begins on Maghe Sankranti, the first day of Magh in the Nepali calendar, which usually falls on 14 or 15 January, and runs as a fair for several days. The organisers announce the exact dates and programme each year. Check current status before you travel and book rooms early.

faqs.q: What happens at the Maghe Sankranti mela?
faqs.a: Devotees take a ritual bath in the Rangeet in the morning. Then the riverbank becomes a fair, with stalls selling food, crafts and household goods, cultural programmes, music and amusement rides. Seasonal foods include sesame sweets, yam, sweet potato and sel roti. Families come from across the region.

faqs.q: Is the mela suitable for families with children?
faqs.a: Yes, children usually love the rides, food and music. Crowds can be heavy at peak times, so agree a meeting point, keep small children close and carry water and snacks. January days at Jorethang's low altitude are mild, around 18–22 °C, with cool mornings.

experiences.title: An evening by the Rangeet at Jorethang
experiences.summary: A short, easy stroll down to the river after a long drive: the wide Rangeet, the bridge to the Darjeeling side, and the hills turning gold as the sun drops. A gentle break in a day of hairpin bends, best in the dry winter months.
body: The Rangeet rises in the mountains of West Sikkim and flows past Legship and Jorethang before joining the Teesta at Tribeni. At Jorethang it is a broad river in a warm valley, and for much of its course it marks the boundary between Sikkim and Darjeeling district.

Walk down from the bazaar to the riverbank in the late afternoon. In winter the water runs clear and green-blue over stones, and local families come down to sit and talk. Watch the light change on the hills to the west, then head back for tea and pakoras in town.

This is a relaxed stop, not an expedition. In the monsoon, from June to September, the river rises fast and turns brown and dangerous; keep well back from the banks and do not wade at any time of year. Carry a bag for rubbish and leave the riverside cleaner than you found it.

faqs.q: Is it safe to swim in the Rangeet at Jorethang?
faqs.a: We advise against it. The Rangeet is cold, has strong currents and can rise quickly after rain upstream, even on a sunny day in town. In the monsoon it is dangerous. Enjoy the riverbank, but do not wade or swim, and keep children well away from the water's edge.

faqs.q: Which river flows through Jorethang?
faqs.a: The Rangeet, a tributary of the Teesta. It rises in the mountains of West Sikkim, passes Legship and Jorethang, and joins the Teesta at Tribeni. For much of its length it forms the boundary between Sikkim and Darjeeling district of West Bengal.

faqs.q: What is the weather like in Jorethang?
faqs.a: Warm. At about 300 m, winter days are around 18–22 °C, while April to September often passes 30 °C with high humidity. The monsoon brings heavy rain from June to September. October to March is the most comfortable time to linger in town.

experiences.title: Thali, momos and sel roti in Jorethang bazaar
experiences.summary: A practical, tasty stop in the market around Jorethang's taxi stand: a rice thali or momos at a busy local eatery, sel roti and tea from a stall, and seasonal fruit for the road. The kind of lunch that keeps long Sikkim drives cheerful and cheap.
body: Jorethang's bazaar feeds a constant flow of jeep passengers, drivers and shoppers from the villages, so food is quick, fresh and cheap. Simple eateries around the taxi stand serve rice thali with dal, vegetables and pickle, plus momos, chowmein and thukpa.

Look for sel roti, the ring-shaped, slightly sweet rice-flour bread fried in oil, eaten with tea or a potato curry. It is everyday food here and festival food everywhere in Nepali households. Fruit stalls sell local bananas year round and Sikkim mandarins from about November to January.

Choose busy places where food is cooked in front of you, and carry small notes, though UPI is widely accepted in town. A full lunch costs about ₹150–350 per person. Drivers know the best spots: ask yours where they eat.

faqs.q: What is sel roti?
faqs.a: Sel roti is a ring-shaped, slightly sweet bread made from a rice-flour batter and deep-fried. It is a traditional Nepali food made at festivals such as Tihar and Dashain and sold daily in Sikkim's markets. It is eaten with tea, yoghurt or potato curry, and keeps well for a day's travel.

faqs.q: Is there vegetarian food in Jorethang?
faqs.a: Yes. Rice thalis with dal and vegetables, vegetable momos, chowmein, puri with potato curry and sel roti are easy to find. A few eateries are pure vegetarian. Ask whether momo dough contains egg if you avoid it.

faqs.q: How much does lunch cost in Jorethang?
faqs.a: A simple thali or a plate of momos costs roughly ₹100–200, and a full lunch with tea and a sweet about ₹150–350 per person. Prices are indicative and lower than in Gangtok or Pelling. UPI payments are accepted in most shops and eateries.

experiences.title: Up the Rangeet valley to Legship's riverside temple
experiences.summary: A short river-valley drive north from Jorethang to Legship in Gyalshing district, where the Kirateshwar Mahadev temple stands by the Rangeet. A quiet half day, or the first stage of the road to Pelling.
body: From Jorethang the road follows the Rangeet upstream through warm, green valley country, past small farms and villages. After about an hour you reach Legship, a small town where roads branch to Gyalshing, Pelling, Tashiding and Ravangla.

By the river at Legship stands the Kirateshwar Mahadev temple, a Shiva shrine associated with Kirateshwar, the form of Shiva honoured by the Kirat communities of the region. It draws pilgrims in particular at Maha Shivaratri and on Mondays in the month of Shrawan. Most visitors stop for a short darshan and a look at the river.

If you are heading to Pelling, Legship is a natural stop on the way. As a return trip from Namchi or Jorethang it fills a relaxed half day. Dress modestly, remove shoes at the temple and follow local customs. Road conditions change after the monsoon; check current status before you travel.

faqs.q: How far is Legship from Jorethang?
faqs.a: About 25–30 km, roughly an hour by car along the Rangeet valley. A reserved small car for a return half day costs about ₹2,000–3,000, indicative. Shared jeeps from Jorethang to Legship and Gyalshing run through the day for less.

faqs.q: What is the Kirateshwar Mahadev temple?
faqs.a: A Shiva temple on the bank of the Rangeet at Legship in Gyalshing district (West Sikkim), dedicated to Shiva as Kirateshwar, a form honoured by the Kirat communities of the region. It is busiest at Maha Shivaratri and during Shrawan. Visitors are welcome; dress modestly and remove shoes.

faqs.q: Can we go on from Legship to Pelling?
faqs.a: Yes. Legship lies on the main Jorethang–Pelling road. From Legship, Pelling is roughly 25 km and an hour further via Gyalshing. The whole Jorethang–Pelling drive is about 50 km and 2 hours, so a temple stop at Legship adds little time.

faqs.q: Is Jorethang worth visiting?
faqs.a: Mainly as a junction and for the Maghe Sankranti mela in mid-January. Jorethang is a practical town for changing jeeps, cash, lunch and fuel, with a pleasant riverfront. Outside mela time, most travellers stop for an hour or two and stay the night in Namchi, 18 km uphill.

faqs.q: How do I get from Siliguri to Jorethang?
faqs.a: Shared jeeps run from Siliguri to Jorethang in about 3.5–4 hours for roughly ₹250–350 a seat, mostly in the morning. A reserved car from NJP or Bagdogra takes 3.5–4 hours and costs about ₹4,500–6,000. When NH10 is closed, vehicles come via Darjeeling district. Check current status before you travel.

faqs.q: How far is Jorethang from Namchi?
faqs.a: About 18 km, roughly 40 minutes by car up a winding road from about 300 m to 1,500 m. Shared jeeps run frequently for about ₹50–80 a seat, and a reserved small car costs about ₹1,000–1,500, indicative.

faqs.q: How far is Jorethang from Pelling?
faqs.a: About 50 km and 2 hours via Legship and Gyalshing. Shared jeeps to Gyalshing or Pelling cost about ₹150–250 a seat, and a reserved car about ₹2,500–3,500 one way. The road climbs steadily from the warm Rangeet valley to Pelling at about 2,150 m.

faqs.q: When is the Maghe Sankranti mela in Jorethang?
faqs.a: It starts on the first day of the Nepali month of Magh, usually 14 or 15 January, and runs for several days as a fair on the Rangeet riverbank. It has been held since 1961. The organisers announce dates each year, so check current status before you travel.

faqs.q: Is there an ATM in Jorethang?
faqs.a: Yes, several banks have ATMs in Jorethang, and UPI is widely accepted in shops and eateries. It is a good place to withdraw cash before heading to remote villages in West or South Sikkim, where ATMs are scarce and cards rarely work.

faqs.q: What is the weather in Jorethang?
faqs.a: Warm for Sikkim. At about 300 m, winter days are mild at roughly 18–22 °C, and April to September is hot and humid, often over 30 °C. Heavy monsoon rain falls from June to September. Snow never falls here. October to March is the most pleasant time.

faqs.q: Do we need a permit for Jorethang?
faqs.a: Indian nationals need no permit. Foreign nationals need the standard Sikkim Restricted Area Permit, applied online through the e-FRRO portal after arriving in India since January 2026. Jorethang is not a protected area. Check current status before you travel.

faqs.q: What if NH10 is closed on the way to South Sikkim?
faqs.a: NH10 between Sevoke and Melli closes after monsoon slides. The usual alternative for South and West Sikkim is to drive from Siliguri through Darjeeling district down to Jorethang, which adds an hour or two. Our drivers check road news each morning. Check current status before you travel.
